answer.evidence: The stair is drawn as a front-on elevation. The frame sits at the top (rows 3-7) with a dark opening below (rows 8-14). Below that, three stacked steps each show a 1-row light edge line (rows 15, 19, 24) over a 3-4 row vertical riser. No step tread is deeper than 1 row, so there is no top surface of 3 or more rows. The left and right frame posts are thin vertical strips, and the silhouette is almost a full rectangle, 29 px wide and 26 rows tall. It does not read as a flat plate seen from above, and it shows no 3/4-view top plane.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a single tile-sized stair frame (about 20x17 source pixels) on a dark backdrop. It is not the 4x3 ground patch the kind calls for, so it cannot be compared to the grass and paving references as a surface. The measured facts are 7 visible tones per tile, matching the paving reference, and 0% near-flat coverage. However, 100% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so the outline reads as a uniform neutral dark line, the 'sticker' look, rather than a tinted material tone. The frame has only about 4 lightness steps. The dark stair interior is a few stacked bands with little grain. By eye it looks thinner and flatter than the paving reference, which has per-stone shading and highlighted joints. It lacks the clustered grain and texture that Beodeul pieces carry. With the neutral outline, the shallow ramps and the doubt about kind, it fails.
